summary:
**Welwitschia Lunar** is an educational Web-based Virtual Reality (**WebVR**) simulator—available entirely in Portuguese and fully functional **offline**—designed to teach astronomy and space sciences to Angolan children aged 7 and older.

Players step into the role of commander of Angola’s first lunar base, managing scarce resources (energy, life support, thermal shielding, food, and scientific research) while navigating conditions modeled on real NASA data—including $1/6\text{th}$ gravity, 14-day lunar nights, extreme temperature swings, and solar storms.

The project directly tackles the challenge of democratizing STEM education by removing three critical barriers: abstract textbook instruction, the English language barrier, and the lack of physical laboratories or reliable internet. Running directly inside a standard web browser, it requires neither continuous connectivity nor expensive hardware.

With one of the world’s youngest populations (roughly 5.4 million children in the primary school age group), Angola holds immense untapped scientific potential. By turning childhood curiosity into hands-on learning through cause and effect, Welwitschia Lunar sparks early interest in STEM careers and inspires the next generation of the Angolan space program.
details:
What does it do or how does it work? Welwitschia Lunar is an educational 3D Web-based Virtual Reality (WebVR) simulator where children aged 7 and older (with a primary focus on ages 7 to 12) take command of Angola’s first lunar base. The experience guides players through a hands-on 7-stage learning journey:

  1. Instant Web Access: Players open the simulator directly inside a standard web browser—with no complex installations required—and choose between immersive VR headset mode or 360° on-screen view.
  2. Lunar Briefing & 360° Exploration: Players receive their mission in clear Portuguese ($384,400\text{ km}$ from Earth) and explore the lunar environment in 360°, identifying solar panels, greenhouses, the lunar surface, and Earth on the horizon.
  3. Resource Management: At each cycle, players allocate limited power across four vital systems: Life Support (oxygen and water), Shielding (radiation and thermal protection), Food (greenhouses), and Science (research operations).
  4. Real NASA Data & Events: Players face authentic lunar conditions modeled on official NASA datasets, including $1/6\text{th}$ gravity, ~14-Earth-day lunar nights, extreme temperature swings ($-173\,^\circ\text{C}$ to $+127\,^\circ\text{C}$), and solar storms.
  5. Cause, Effect & Achievement: Every decision produces an immediate impact on crew health and station stability. Upon completing the mission, players unlock astronomy facts, and progress is saved locally on the device (localStorage), ensuring 100% offline functionality.

What benefits does it have?

  • Universal Accessibility (100% Offline & Web-Based): Runs directly in a standard browser without requiring continuous internet access, supercomputers, or expensive consoles, overcoming the lack of physical science laboratories and reliable home connectivity.
  • Linguistic Inclusion: Interface, narrative, and scientific glossary are built entirely in Portuguese, removing the English-language barrier that distances young learners from traditional space education tools.
  • Active Learning by Cause and Effect: Instead of memorizing formulas or abstract texts, children understand real engineering trade-offs and develop critical thinking through hands-on decision-making.
  • Space-to-Earth Sustainability: By managing solar energy, water, and agriculture on a lunar base, children learn sustainability principles directly applicable to real environmental challenges in Angola.

What is the intended impact of the project? Angola has one of the youngest populations in the world, with approximately 5.4 million children aged 7 to 12 in primary and lower secondary education. The project aims to:

  • Kick off practical field validation in Luanda with at least 100 children, scaling progressively through science clubs, tech communities, and institutional partnerships across all 21 provinces of Angola.
  • Democratize access to STEM and astronomy education starting in primary school, sparking early scientific vocations and inspiring the next generation of engineers and scientists for Angola’s national space program (GGPEN) and global missions such as NASA’s Artemis Program.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Web & 3D/VR Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, TypeScript/JavaScript, React, and Three.js with WebVR / WebXR support (physically based rendering [PBR] of the lunar surface, rover physics, circular navigation radar, and stereoscopic viewing for mobile VR headsets and 360° mode), alongside Portuguese speech-synthesis APIs for the virtual co-pilot (Welly) and localStorage for 100% offline data persistence.
  • Design, Art & Modeling: 3D modeling tools, child-friendly UI/UX design tools, digital illustration software, and visual identity design to create an intuitive and welcoming space environment.
  • Scientific Datasets: Official physical parameters sourced from the NASA Moon Fact Sheet and Artemis Program documentation.
  • Hardware: Standard laptops for development and testing, and everyday smartphones or computers with a web browser (with or without simple mobile VR headsets) for end-user gameplay.

How is your project creative?

  • Cultural Identity & Symbolism: The name Welwitschia Lunar draws inspiration from Welwitschia mirabilis, an endemic plant of Angola’s Namib Desert renowned for its extreme resilience with scarce resources—serving as a direct metaphor for human survival on a lunar base.
  • Children in Command: While most space apps merely display static sky maps or passive videos, Welwitschia Lunar places the child at the center of the action as commander of an Angolan lunar outpost.
  • Interactive Co-Pilot & Dynamic Dilemmas: Replaces traditional quizzes with dynamic engineering dilemmas, immediate feedback, and interactive guidance in Portuguese.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Local Infrastructure & Connectivity: Data from UNICEF and the ITU show that 2.2 billion children and young people worldwide lack internet access at home; therefore, the project architecture prioritized 100% offline functionality and lightweight performance for mobile devices and everyday browsers.
  • Age Appropriateness & Cognitive Load: The team balanced scientific rigor from real NASA datasets with accessible language and clear, playful visuals, ensuring space science is neither intimidating nor oversimplified.
  • Multidisciplinary Execution & Scalability: The project integrated management, WebVR engineering, scientific modeling, simulation rules (game design), and child-centered aesthetics, while establishing a hybrid sustainability model combining free community access with school licensing and institutional sponsorships.
